name: Amethyst
mineral: Quartz variety (silicon dioxide) coloured by iron and natural irradiation
colors: pale lilac to deep royal violet, often zoned with clear quartz
description: Its name comes from the Greek amethystos, 'not drunk', for the ancient belief that a cup carved of it kept the drinker sober. Bishops wore it in their rings as a sign of spiritual sobriety, and it was once valued as highly as diamond until vast Brazilian deposits were found in the 1800s. The violet glow of a geode cave has long been seen as a doorway to the quiet places of the mind.
metaphysicalUses: Amethyst is the witch's stone of the clear and watchful mind. It quiets mental chatter so intuition can be heard, guards against psychic attack and nightmares, and helps break cycles of addiction or overindulgence. Placed on the brow it opens the inner eye for divination and trance; kept beside the bed it calls prophetic, gentle dreams. Many keep an amethyst point on the altar as a general spiritual guardian and amplifier of prayer and meditation.
uses: Tuck a tumbled amethyst under your pillow to soften nightmares and invite prophetic dreams
Hold it to the third eye during meditation or scrying to deepen trance
Place a cluster in the center of the home to keep the atmosphere calm and watchful
Carry one in a pocket as a sobriety talisman when resisting a craving
Set it beside tarot cards overnight to attune the deck
Grid four points around the bed for psychic protection during sleep
substituteNotes: Clear Quartz carries the same quartz amplification, while lilac Lepidolite, Fluorite and Charoite share amethyst's calming, intuitive purple ray.
cleansing: Water-safe for brief rinses (hardness 7). Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight or by resting on selenite. NOT sun-safe: prolonged sunlight fades its violet; charge under the moon instead.
whereToFind: Brazil and Uruguay produce the great geodes; also Zambia, Madagascar, Mexico (Veracruz and Guerrero), Canada (Thunder Bay) and South Korea. Buy from sellers who can name the mine and avoid heat-treated 'citrine' passed off as natural.
caution: Fades with prolonged sun exposure; keep it out of bright windows. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Late winter, Imbolc through the Spring Equinox (Feb–Mar), the season of Pisces
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Clear Quartz
mineral: Quartz (silicon dioxide)
colors: water-clear to milky white, sometimes with rainbows, phantoms or inclusions
description: The Greeks called it krystallos, believing it was ice frozen so deeply by the gods that it could never thaw. Crystal balls, Celtic charm stones and the healing crystals of Aboriginal and Native American medicine people were all fashioned from it. Its piezoelectric nature, which makes it vibrate under pressure, keeps time in modern watches, a fitting echo of its old reputation as the stone that holds and transmits energy.
metaphysicalUses: Clear quartz is the universal amplifier, the blank page of the mineral kingdom. It takes on whatever intention is programmed into it and magnifies it, and it boosts the power of herbs, candles and other stones placed near it. Use it as a stand-in for any crystal you lack, as a wand to direct energy, as a scrying sphere, or as the central stone of any grid. It clears muddy thinking and lifts the energy of a room.
uses: Program a point by holding it, breathing your intention onto it and speaking it aloud
Place at the center of a crystal grid to link and amplify the surrounding stones
Use a quartz point as a wand to cast circles and direct energy
Gaze into a sphere by candlelight for scrying
Set beside a spell candle to strengthen its working
Add to a charm bag as a general amplifier of every other ingredient
substituteNotes: Herkimer and Danburite share quartz's crystalline clarity and high vibration, Selenite echoes its purity, and Smoky Quartz is quartz grounded in earth.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe; cleanse in running water, salt water (rinse afterwards), sunlight, moonlight, smoke or sound. Note that a polished sphere in sunlight can focus rays and start a fire.
whereToFind: Found worldwide; famous sources include Arkansas (USA), Brazil, Madagascar, the Swiss Alps and the Himalayas. Look for small-scale miners and avoid glass sold as quartz (glass feels warmer and often has bubbles).
caution: Never leave a clear quartz sphere in direct sun near flammables; it can act as a burning lens. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Any time of year; especially strong at the Summer Solstice (Litha, June) when the sun is at its peak
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Rose Quartz
mineral: Quartz variety (silicon dioxide) coloured by microscopic dumortierite-like fibres
colors: soft blush to warm rose pink, translucent to milky
description: Greek legend says Aphrodite cut herself on a briar while rushing to save Adonis, and her blood mingled with his to stain white quartz pink. Rose quartz beads have been found in Mesopotamian sites dating to 7000 BCE, and Egyptians and Romans used it in facial masks believed to prevent wrinkles. It is the gentle, maternal stone of the heart in nearly every modern tradition.
metaphysicalUses: Rose quartz opens the heart softly. It is worked to draw romantic love, but its deeper gift is self-love and forgiveness, which makes all other love possible. It soothes grief, heals old heart wounds, restores trust after betrayal and calms quarrels in the household. Add it to love spells, honey jars, glamour work and bath rituals, or keep it near anyone who is grieving.
uses: Place a pair of rose quartz stones in the relationship corner of your bedroom to invite love
Drop a tumbled stone in a love-drawing bath (it is water-safe)
Hold over the heart while speaking kind words to yourself in a mirror
Add to a honey jar sweetening spell for reconciliation
Give a tumbled stone to a grieving friend as a comfort talisman
Rest on the face during a glamour or beauty ritual
substituteNotes: Pink Rhodochrosite, Morganite, Kunzite and Rhodonite all carry heart-healing love energy, and Green Aventurine works the heart chakra through its green ray.
cleansing: Water-safe for rinsing. Cleanse with moonlight, smoke or sound. Limit sunlight, as its pink can fade over time; charge under a waxing or full moon.
whereToFind: Brazil, Madagascar, South Africa, India and South Dakota (USA). Widely available; dyed quartz and pink glass are common fakes, so buy from reputable sellers.
caution: Color may fade in prolonged direct sunlight. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Spring into early summer, Beltane (May 1) and around Valentine's Day in February; Fridays, Venus's day
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Smoky Quartz
mineral: Quartz variety (silicon dioxide) darkened by natural irradiation of aluminium impurities
colors: pale smoke-grey to deep brown and near-black (morion)
description: Smoky quartz is the national gem of Scotland, where it is called Cairngorm after the mountains where it was found and set into the hilts of sgian-dubh daggers and kilt brooches. Druids were said to revere it as a stone of the earth gods. Twelfth-century Chinese judges wore smoky quartz lenses as the first sunglasses, hiding their expressions in court.
metaphysicalUses: Smoky quartz draws scattered, anxious energy down into the earth and transmutes it. It is the stone to hold after intense ritual, spirit work or a hard day, and to place at doorways to absorb negativity before it enters. It helps release old habits and fears, supports shadow work without overwhelm, and lends calm courage. Unlike black stones that block, smoky quartz filters and neutralises.
uses: Hold in the left hand after ritual to ground excess energy
Place on the windowsill or by the front door to filter negativity
Keep on your desk near electronics for a calmer workspace
Use as a focus stone when writing release lists to burn at the waning moon
Carry during stressful travel or exams to stay level
Set at the four corners of a property as earthly protection
substituteNotes: Black Tourmaline, Obsidian, Hematite and Apache Tear share its grounding and protective root energy, while Clear Quartz carries the same quartz structure.
cleansing: Water-safe; cleanse in running water, earth (bury overnight), smoke or sound. Can fade with prolonged strong sunlight, so prefer moonlight or burying in soil.
whereToFind: Scotland (Cairngorms), the Swiss Alps, Brazil, Madagascar, Colorado and Arkansas (USA). Beware artificially irradiated clear quartz that is very dark and uniform.
caution: Can fade with prolonged strong sunlight; some smoky quartz is artificially irradiated, which is not a hazard but should be labeled. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Late autumn, Samhain (Oct 31) to the Winter Solstice (Nov–Dec)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Citrine
mineral: Quartz variety (silicon dioxide) coloured by iron; much commercial citrine is heat-treated amethyst
colors: pale champagne to honey gold and deep madeira orange
description: Named from the French citron, lemon, citrine has been carved into jewellery since the Hellenistic age and was popular with Scottish weavers for brooches and sword hilts. Shopkeepers traditionally kept a piece in the cash box, earning it the name Merchant's Stone. Natural citrine is rare and pale; most bright orange 'citrine' clusters on the market are baked amethyst.
metaphysicalUses: Citrine carries the warmth of the sun into money magic and personal power. It draws prosperity, success in business and opportunities, and it is said to never need cleansing because it does not hold negativity. It brightens moods, lifts depression, stokes creativity and strengthens willpower at the solar plexus. Use it in money jars, prosperity grids, job-seeking spells and anywhere you want joyful, generous energy.
uses: Keep a piece in your wallet, till or cash box to draw money
Place in the far-left corner of your home or desk (the wealth corner in feng shui)
Add to a money-drawing jar with cinnamon, basil and a coin
Hold while visualising goals at the waxing moon
Wear as a pendant at the solar plexus for confidence in interviews
Set on a business card or invoice to bless a new venture
substituteNotes: Golden Pyrite, Sunstone, Tiger's Eye and Orange Calcite share citrine's solar, prosperous fire, and Green Aventurine is the other great luck-and-money stone.
cleansing: Water-safe. Natural citrine can pale with long sun exposure despite its solar nature; brief morning sun is fine. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight.
whereToFind: Natural citrine comes from Brazil, the Democratic Republic of Congo (Kundelungu), Madagascar, Russia and Spain. Ask whether stones are heated; natural citrine is pale and evenly smoky-gold, while heated amethyst is orange with white bases.
caution: Most deep-orange citrine is heat-treated amethyst; it still works magically, but buy knowingly. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: High summer, Litha to Lughnasadh (Jun–Aug); Sundays and Thursdays
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Ametrine
mineral: Quartz variety (silicon dioxide) with amethyst and citrine zones in one crystal
colors: violet and golden yellow zones meeting in a sharp line
description: Nearly all ametrine comes from the Anahí mine in Bolivia. Legend says a 17th-century Spanish conquistador received the mine as dowry when he married Anahí, a princess of the Ayoreo people, and she gave him a piece of ametrine as she died, defending her husband from her own tribe. Its two colours form where heat differences within a single crystal leave some iron in one oxidation state and some in another.
metaphysicalUses: Ametrine marries the spiritual vision of amethyst with the solar will of citrine. It is the stone for turning inspiration into action, balancing dreams with practicality, and harmonising opposites within the self or in a partnership. It clears confusion, supports decisions, and helps the spiritual seeker who also needs to pay the rent. Use it when your magic needs both inner knowing and outward success.
uses: Hold during meditation then journal practical steps, letting both colours speak
Place between photos of two people to harmonise a partnership
Carry when making major decisions for clarity and confidence
Use on a prosperity altar where spiritual work and money work meet
Rest on the solar plexus with the purple end toward the head to align will and intuition
substituteNotes: Pair Amethyst and Citrine together to recreate its duality, or use Clear Quartz or multicoloured Fluorite for clarity and balance.
cleansing: Water-safe. Avoid long sunlight as both colour zones may fade. Cleanse with moonlight, smoke or sound.
whereToFind: Almost exclusively the Anahí mine in eastern Bolivia; small amounts from Brazil and India. Synthetic ametrine exists; reputable gem dealers can confirm origin.
caution: Can fade in prolonged sunlight. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: The equinoxes, Ostara (Mar) and Mabon (Sep), when day and night stand in balance
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Herkimer Diamond
mineral: Double-terminated quartz (silicon dioxide), not a true diamond
colors: brilliantly water-clear, sometimes with black carbon or oil inclusions
description: These naturally faceted, double-pointed quartz crystals grow in pockets of 500-million-year-old dolomite near Herkimer County, New York. The Mohawk people knew them long before European settlers, and canal workers in the 1700s were astonished to find 'diamonds' lying in the turned soil. They form in voids that let them grow freely in all directions, giving them their gemmy clarity.
metaphysicalUses: Herkimer diamonds are among the most potent quartz for vision, dreams and attunement. Their two points send and receive energy, making them ideal for astral travel, lucid dreaming and telepathic connection. They amplify other stones, help recall dreams and past-life memories, and cleanse the aura. Pairs of Herkimers are given to friends or lovers to stay energetically linked across distance.
uses: Place under the pillow or tape to the headboard for vivid, remembered dreams
Give one of a matching pair to a distant loved one to keep a link
Set at the crown during astral travel or journeying
Add to elixirs indirectly (in a sealed vial in water) to charge water with clarity
Use as the amplifying heart stone of a grid
Hold during spell work to sharpen focus and intent
substituteNotes: Clear Quartz is the same mineral, Danburite and Selenite share its high crystalline clarity, and Amethyst serves its dream-work gifts.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe. Cleanse in running water, sunlight, moonlight, smoke or sound.
whereToFind: Herkimer County and the Mohawk River valley in New York, USA, where you can dig your own at fee-dig mines. Similar double-terminated quartz from Pakistan and Mexico is sometimes mislabelled.
caution: Some sensitive people find it overstimulating at bedtime, so start small. It is quartz (hardness 7), not diamond. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Early winter, Yule (Dec), season of Sagittarius dreaming
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Black Tourmaline
mineral: Tourmaline group, schorl (complex sodium iron aluminium borosilicate)
colors: opaque glossy black with deep vertical striations
description: Tourmaline comes from the Sinhalese turmali, meaning mixed gems. Dutch traders called it aschentrekker, 'ash puller', because warmed tourmaline becomes electrically charged and pulls ash from pipes, a property called pyroelectricity. Magicians of old Africa and the Americas used black tourmaline as a shield against evil spirits and ill-wishing.
metaphysicalUses: Black tourmaline is the cornerstone protection stone of modern witchcraft. It repels and transmutes negative energy, ill-will, psychic attack and curses, sending them down into the earth. It grounds the spirit firmly in the body, steadies the anxious, and is said to buffer electromagnetic smog. Use it in protection jars, at the boundaries of the home, and in any hex-breaking or uncrossing work.
uses: Place one by each door and window to ward the home
Add to a witch bottle or protection jar with salt, rosemary and pins
Carry in the left pocket when entering difficult places
Grid four stones at the corners of your bed or property
Hold during cord-cutting or uncrossing rituals
Keep beside your computer or phone to buffer harsh energy
substituteNotes: Obsidian, Shungite, Jet and Black Onyx are all powerful black shielding stones, and Smoky Quartz offers gentler grounding.
cleansing: Water-safe for quick rinses, though its striations can trap water and rough pieces may flake; dry well. Cleanse with smoke, earth, sound or selenite. Sun-safe. Cleanse often, as it absorbs a lot.
whereToFind: Brazil, Pakistan, Namibia, Madagascar, Afghanistan and the USA (Maine, California). Choose sellers who source from artisanal mines; it is inexpensive, so avoid painted or dyed fakes.
caution: Raw pieces can shed sharp splinters; handle carefully. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Samhain (Oct 31) and the dark half of the year (Nov–Jan)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Obsidian
mineral: Volcanic glass (amorphous, mostly silicon dioxide); a mineraloid
colors: glassy jet-black, sometimes with gold or silver sheen, mahogany or rainbow banding
description: Born when lava cools too fast to crystallise, obsidian was humanity's first scalpel and arrowhead. The Aztecs dedicated it to Tezcatlipoca, the 'Smoking Mirror', and Dr John Dee, astrologer to Elizabeth I, scried with an Aztec obsidian mirror now held in the British Museum. Its glassy blade-edge has made it a stone of truth that cuts through illusion.
metaphysicalUses: Obsidian is a black mirror for the soul. It reflects back what we hide, which makes it powerful for shadow work, uncovering truth and cutting cords to people or patterns. As a scrying mirror it is one of the oldest tools of divination and spirit contact. It forms a strong protective shield, absorbing hostility and returning it to its source. Its intensity is best balanced with gentler stones and good aftercare.
uses: Scry in a polished obsidian mirror by candlelight on the dark moon
Use an obsidian blade or point to symbolically cut energetic cords
Place by the entrance to absorb hostility from visitors
Hold during shadow work journaling to face hidden truths
Add to a protection or reversal spell to send harm back to its sender
Carry when you need to see through deception
substituteNotes: Snowflake Obsidian and Apache Tear are gentler forms of obsidian, while Black Tourmaline, Jet and Black Onyx carry its protective black power.
cleansing: Brief rinse is safe; dry immediately. Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight or earth. Sun-safe, but avoid sudden temperature changes which can crack glass.
whereToFind: Mexico, Armenia, Iceland, Italy (Lipari), Japan, Oregon and California (USA). Buy from sellers who distinguish real obsidian from black glass (real obsidian often has subtle flow lines and sheen).
caution: Edges can be razor sharp; handle raw pieces and blades carefully. Its intensity can bring up difficult emotions. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Samhain (Oct 31) through the dark of winter (Nov–Dec)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Snowflake Obsidian
mineral: Volcanic glass with radial cristobalite inclusions
colors: black glass scattered with grey-white 'snowflake' blooms
description: The white flowers in snowflake obsidian are clusters of cristobalite that crystallise as the glass slowly ages, a stone beginning to remember order inside chaos. It is often called the stone of purity and of balance, with darkness and light held together. Utah is one of its classic sources.
metaphysicalUses: Snowflake obsidian offers the honesty of obsidian with a gentler hand. Its white flakes are reminders that even in darkness there is light, which makes it beloved for shadow work, recovering from hard times, and breaking negative thought patterns. It calms, grounds, and helps one see mistakes as lessons. Use it in winter rituals, rest and recovery work, and meditation on the balance of light and dark.
uses: Meditate with it at Yule, contemplating the light born in darkness
Carry during periods of grief or isolation for steady support
Use as a gentler scrying stone for beginners
Place on the root chakra to calm and ground after stress
Write a habit you are releasing and lay the stone on the paper overnight
substituteNotes: Obsidian and Apache Tear are the same volcanic glass, Smoky Quartz grounds and filters, and Howlite echoes its calming black-and-white balance.
cleansing: Brief water rinse is fine; dry well. Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight. Sun-safe.
whereToFind: Utah and Nevada (USA), Mexico. Widely available and inexpensive; support rockhound co-ops where possible.
caution: Chipped edges can be sharp like glass. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Midwinter, Yule (Dec 21) through Imbolc (Feb 1)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Apache Tear
mineral: Rounded nodules of obsidian (volcanic glass) weathered from perlite
colors: opaque black that glows translucent smoky brown when held to light
description: A legend from the American Southwest tells of Apache warriors who rode off a cliff rather than be captured by cavalry, and of the women whose tears turned to black stones where they fell. Hold an Apache tear to the light and it turns translucent, a sign that grief, too, can let light through. Many feel the name and legend should be shared with respect for the Apache peoples.
metaphysicalUses: Apache tear is the gentle companion of mourning. It absorbs sorrow, helps tears flow and dry, and brings understanding of loss without the harshness of black obsidian. It is a protective amulet and a grounding stone, and it is kept on ancestor altars and carried through funerals and anniversaries. Use it in release rituals, grief work, and to forgive oneself and others.
uses: Carry in a pocket through a funeral or anniversary of a loss
Place on an ancestor altar beside photographs and offerings
Hold to candlelight and watch it become translucent while speaking of the departed
Rest on the heart and cry freely, then cleanse the stone in smoke
Gift to someone grieving with a written blessing
substituteNotes: Snowflake and black Obsidian are the same glass, Smoky Quartz grounds sorrow, and Rose Quartz offers the heart-comfort grief needs.
cleansing: Water-safe briefly. Cleanse with smoke, earth or moonlight after grief work. Sun-safe.
whereToFind: Arizona and New Mexico (USA) and Mexico, weathering out of perlite deposits. Inexpensive; buy from local rock shops that respect the stone's cultural story.
caution: Chipped edges can be sharp like glass. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Autumn, Mabon to Samhain (Sep–Oct), the season of remembering the dead
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Black Onyx
mineral: Chalcedony (microcrystalline quartz); most black onyx is dyed agate
colors: uniform deep black, sometimes with white bands
description: Onyx comes from the Greek for fingernail; myth says Eros clipped the nails of sleeping Aphrodite and the Fates turned the clippings to stone so no part of a goddess would perish. Medieval lore warned it could stir quarrels between lovers, while Roman soldiers carried carved onyx for courage in battle. Nearly all jet-black onyx sold today is chalcedony dyed using an ancient sugar-and-acid process.
metaphysicalUses: Black onyx is a stone of discipline, self-mastery and steady strength. It absorbs and contains negativity, helps keep secrets, and grants the stamina to see hard tasks through. It is used in banishing, protection and binding, and to close chapters with finality. Its Saturnian energy lends structure and resolve to anyone who tends to scatter their power.
uses: Wear as a ring or pendant to hold your boundaries in difficult company
Use in banishing spells on a Saturday at the waning moon
Carry during hard physical or mental labour for stamina
Place on a binding or secret-keeping charm
Hold during a ritual ending a relationship or job
substituteNotes: Black Tourmaline, Obsidian, Jet and Shungite share its protective blackness, and Hematite matches its grounding strength.
cleansing: Water-safe; cleanse with running water, smoke or earth. Sun-safe.
whereToFind: Brazil, India, Uruguay, Mexico and Madagascar. Assume black onyx is dyed unless stated; natural banded onyx is available from reputable gem dealers.
caution: Most black onyx is dyed chalcedony; the dye is stable but avoid harsh chemicals. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Winter, Yule through Imbolc (Dec–Jan), the season of Capricorn; Saturdays
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Hematite
mineral: Iron oxide (Fe2O3)
colors: metallic silver-grey to black; streaks and powders blood red
description: Hematite takes its name from the Greek haima, blood, for the red streak it leaves and the red water it produces when cut. Ground hematite is red ochre, the pigment of the Lascaux cave paintings and of burials dating back tens of thousands of years. Roman soldiers rubbed it on their bodies for invulnerability in battle, and it has been carried for courage ever since.
metaphysicalUses: Hematite pulls you down into your body and the solid earth. It is the go-to grounding stone after spirit work or astral travel, and it sharpens focus, memory and logical thinking. Its mirror-like surface reflects negativity back to its source, and it lends Martial courage and stamina. Use it to centre before ritual, to steady the anxious, and in protection and strength magic.
uses: Hold one in each hand to ground after meditation or ritual
Carry during exams or study for focus and memory
Place at the feet during a healing session to anchor the body
Use as a reflective shield in a protection jar
Wear as a bracelet for courage in confrontation
Draw a red ochre line with hematite powder to mark sacred space (use ready-made ochre pigment rather than grinding stone yourself, work outdoors, and do not breathe the dust)
substituteNotes: Smoky Quartz and Black Tourmaline ground and protect, Lodestone is magnetic iron oxide, and Shungite and Pyrite carry its metallic earth energy.
cleansing: NOT water-safe: it can rust and develop red spots. Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight or on selenite. Sun-safe.
whereToFind: Brazil, Australia, Morocco, England (Cumbria), Michigan and Minnesota (USA). Note that much shiny 'hematite' jewellery is 'hematine', a synthetic magnetic material.
caution: Not water-safe (may rust). Magnetic 'hematite' jewelry is usually synthetic; keep it away from pacemakers and other implanted devices, and keep magnetic beads away from children. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Early spring, the season of Aries (Mar–Apr); Tuesdays
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Jet
mineral: Fossilised wood (lignite, an organic mineraloid)
colors: deep velvety black to dark brown, warm to the touch
description: Jet is wood of the monkey-puzzle trees' ancestors, crushed beneath the sea for 180 million years. Bronze Age Britons buried their dead with jet beads, and Whitby jet became the jewel of mourning after Queen Victoria wore it for Prince Albert. Paired with amber in the ceremonial necklaces of high priestesses, it is the dark half of an old witch's set; like amber, it builds static when rubbed.
metaphysicalUses: Jet is an ancient protective amulet against the evil eye, nightmares and malicious spirits, and it absorbs grief tenderly. Because it was once living wood, it is said to hold a deep memory of the earth and of time, making it a stone for ancestor work and contact with the dead. Wear jet with amber to balance dark and light, the traditional regalia of a high priestess.
uses: Wear a jet and amber necklace during rituals of the Goddess
Place on an ancestor or mourning altar
Keep under a child's bed or crib as a traditional protection against nightmares (out of reach)
Use as a talisman against the evil eye
Rub gently to raise a small static charge before casting, as the old witches did
substituteNotes: Obsidian, Black Tourmaline and Black Onyx share jet's protective blackness, Apache Tear carries its grief work, and Amber is its organic sister.
cleansing: Soft and porous: NOT water-safe for soaking, and avoid salt and sunlight which can crack or dull it. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight; wipe with a soft dry cloth.
whereToFind: Whitby on the Yorkshire coast (England), Asturias (Spain), Poland, Turkey and Colorado (USA). Black glass ('French jet') and plastic are common fakes; true jet is very light and warm.
caution: Soft and fragile; keep away from water, heat and harsh chemicals. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Samhain (Oct 31) and the dark weeks before Yule (Nov–Dec)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Shungite
mineral: Carbon-rich mineraloid (up to 98% carbon in elite shungite), containing fullerenes
colors: matte to silvery-lustrous black
description: Shungite is found almost only near the village of Shunga by Lake Onega in Karelia, Russia, and is around two billion years old. Peter the Great is said to have founded Russia's first spa at Marcial Waters, where springs flowed through shungite, and soldiers drank from them. Its natural fullerene molecules have made it a darling of both researchers and the crystal world.
metaphysicalUses: Shungite is a powerful absorber and purifier of energy. It is used to shield against negative and chaotic energies, to cleanse other crystals, and to ground. Many witches place it near electronics, at the threshold, or in protection grids. Elite (silvery) shungite is regarded as the most potent. Its very ancient, carbon-based nature links it to the primordial earth and the life force.
uses: Keep a shungite plate or pyramid beside computers and routers
Lay other crystals on a shungite slab to cleanse them
Carry a piece in your pocket as an energetic shield
Grid shungite at the corners of a room before a cleansing ritual
Place in the soil of a houseplant pot to symbolically purify the home's energy
substituteNotes: Black Tourmaline, Obsidian and Jet shield and absorb as shungite does, while Hematite and Smoky Quartz ground.
cleansing: Regular shungite tolerates brief rinses; elite shungite is brittle and best cleansed with smoke, sound or earth. Sun-safe. Many sellers say it never needs cleansing, but rinsing or smoking it is still wise.
whereToFind: Karelia region of Russia (Zazhoginskoye deposit). Supply chains can be murky and some 'shungite' is dyed or other black rock; buy elite shungite from established dealers.
caution: Leaves black dust on hands. Do not drink shungite-infused water; health claims are unproven, and pieces can shed particles and trace metals. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Late autumn into winter (Nov–Jan)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Selenite
mineral: Gypsum, crystalline variety (hydrated calcium sulfate); most 'selenite wands' are satin spar gypsum
colors: translucent white to pearl, with a silky, moonlike sheen
description: Selenite is named for Selene, the Greek goddess of the Moon, for its pale moonlike glow. The Giant Crystal Cave of Naica in Mexico holds selenite beams over eleven metres long, grown slowly in hot mineral water for half a million years. Thin, clear sheets were used as window panes in Roman and medieval times, called lapis specularis.
metaphysicalUses: Selenite is the great cleanser of the crystal world. A selenite plate or wand clears and recharges other stones, tools and the aura simply by contact, and it is said to need no cleansing itself. It connects to angels, spirit guides and the moon, brings serene calm and clarity, and fills a space with gentle light. Use it to sweep the aura, consecrate tools and seal a room with peace.
uses: Lay stones, jewellery or tarot cards on a selenite plate overnight to cleanse them
Sweep a wand through the aura from head to toe to clear heavy energy
Place towers in the corners of a room to create a calm protective grid
Hold during meditation to connect with guides
Set on the altar during full moon rites as a moon emblem
substituteNotes: Clear Quartz and Danburite cleanse and clarify, Moonstone carries its lunar energy, and the related sulfates Angelite and Celestite share its angelic serenity.
cleansing: NOT water-safe: it is soft gypsum and will dissolve, pit and lose its sheen in water or salt. Keep it dry. Sun-safe for short periods but can turn brittle. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight.
whereToFind: Morocco (most satin spar wands), Mexico (Naica, Chihuahua), Utah and Oklahoma (USA), Australia. Inexpensive and widely available.
caution: Not water-safe; it slowly dissolves. Very soft and scratches easily; thin pieces break and satin spar splinters can be sharp. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Any season; especially midsummer, the season of Cancer (late Jun–Jul)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Moonstone
mineral: Feldspar (orthoclase and albite intergrowth)
colors: milky white, peach, grey or rainbow, with a floating blue-white glow (adularescence)
description: The Romans believed moonstone was moonlight made solid, and in India it is sacred, said to hold a living spirit whose luck waxes and wanes with the moon. Its shimmer, called adularescence, comes from light scattering between microscopic layers of feldspar. It was a favourite of Art Nouveau jewellers and remains the classic stone of lovers and travellers by night.
metaphysicalUses: Moonstone is the jewel of the Triple Goddess and of lunar magic. It strengthens intuition and psychic gifts, eases the emotional tides of the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and menopause, and blesses new beginnings. It is a traveller's amulet, especially for night journeys and travel by water. Wear it during moon rituals, carry it for fertility, and hold it to welcome lovers and fresh starts.
uses: Wear during esbats to draw down the moon
Carry while travelling, especially at night or over water
Place in a fertility charm bag with an egg shell and rose petals
Tuck under the pillow at the full moon for prophetic dreams
Hold at the new moon while setting intentions for new beginnings
Give as a love token between partners
substituteNotes: Selenite and Pearl are classic lunar stones, Labradorite is its feldspar cousin with similar flash, and Opal and Clear Quartz echo its glow and receptivity.
cleansing: Water-safe for brief rinses, but avoid soaking and salt. Charge under the moon, especially the full moon. Avoid harsh sun and heat, which can dull it.
whereToFind: Sri Lanka, India, Madagascar, Myanmar and Tanzania. 'Rainbow moonstone' is technically white labradorite. Opalite glass is often sold as moonstone; real moonstone shows a moving glow rather than a uniform blue.
caution: Can cleave or crack with knocks; protect rings from hard blows. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Midsummer, the season of Cancer (late Jun–Jul), and every full moon of the year
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Labradorite
mineral: Feldspar (plagioclase, calcium sodium aluminium silicate)
colors: smoky grey-green to dark grey with flashes of peacock blue, gold, green and violet
description: Inuit legend says the aurora borealis was once trapped in the rocks along the coast of Labrador until a warrior struck them with his spear, freeing most of the lights but leaving some locked in the stone. The flash, called labradorescence, comes from light bouncing between thin internal layers. Finnish spectrolite shows the richest full-spectrum colours.
metaphysicalUses: Labradorite is the magician's stone. It awakens latent psychic abilities, shields the aura from energy drains and psychic attack, and protects during deep spiritual work. It reveals hidden truths and helps navigate transformation, bringing light to murky situations. Wear it when doing readings, spirit work or any magic that demands both power and protection.
uses: Wear as a pendant during tarot readings or mediumship to sharpen and shield
Hold during guided journeying or trance
Keep in your workspace if you deal with draining people
Gaze into its flash as a focus for scrying
Place on the altar as an emblem of hidden magic awakened
substituteNotes: Moonstone is its feldspar cousin, Opal and Fire Agate share its play of colour, and Amethyst and Obsidian carry its psychic and protective gifts.
cleansing: Water-safe briefly; dry well. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight. Avoid long, hot sun and harsh chemicals which can dull the polish.
whereToFind: Madagascar, Finland (spectrolite), Canada (Labrador, Newfoundland), Norway and Russia. Plentiful and affordable; check for strong flash in good light.
caution: Can cleave or chip with knocks. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Late autumn and Samhain (Oct–Nov), when the veil is thin
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Lapis Lazuli
mineral: Rock composed mainly of lazurite, with calcite, sodalite and pyrite
colors: deep celestial blue flecked with golden pyrite and white calcite
description: Mined in the Sar-e-Sang mines of Afghanistan for over 6,000 years, lapis lazuli adorned Tutankhamun's death mask and the royal tombs of Ur. In the Sumerian myth, Inanna descended to the underworld wearing a lapis necklace and carrying a lapis measuring rod. Ground into ultramarine, it was the most precious pigment of Renaissance painters, reserved for the Virgin Mary's robes.
metaphysicalUses: Lapis is the royal stone of wisdom and truth. It opens the third eye for insight and the throat for honest, courageous speech. It connects with sacred knowledge, sky deities and the starry heavens, aids study and memory, and protects against psychic attack. Kings, priests and sages wore it to hold divine authority; witches use it in divination, dream work and spells for truth and justice.
uses: Wear at the throat when you must speak truth with authority
Place on the third eye during meditation for insight
Keep on the desk while studying the occult arts
Add to a justice or legal-matters spell for honest outcomes
Set on an altar to sky or star deities
Place under the pillow to remember dreams
substituteNotes: Sodalite and Azurite are close blue stones of the mind, Sapphire carries royal wisdom, Blue Kyanite opens the throat, and Amethyst opens the third eye.
cleansing: Not water-safe for soaking (porous, calcite content, and pyrite can tarnish). Avoid salt and acids. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight. Prolonged sun may fade it slightly.
whereToFind: Badakhshan province, Afghanistan (the classic source), Chile, Russia (Lake Baikal) and Myanmar. Dyed howlite, jasper and sodalite are sold as lapis; Afghan mining can fund conflict, so ask about provenance.
caution: Soft and porous; keep from water and household chemicals. It contains pyrite and calcite, and dyed imitations may bleed color. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Late autumn, season of Sagittarius (late Nov–Dec)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Sodalite
mineral: Sodium aluminium silicate with chlorine (feldspathoid)
colors: royal blue veined with white calcite, sometimes violet
description: Sodalite was named for its sodium content when it was found in Greenland in 1811. It became famous when Princess Patricia of Connaught chose stone from a new Ontario quarry to decorate Marlborough House in London, earning it the name Princess Blue. Unlike lapis, it rarely has golden pyrite and its white veins are bolder.
metaphysicalUses: Sodalite brings logic and intuition into conversation. It calms panic and racing thoughts, encourages rational thought, objectivity and truthful speech, and helps put feelings into words. It is the student's and writer's stone and a soothing companion for anxious speakers. Use it in communication spells, study charms and meditation on inner truth.
uses: Hold before a difficult conversation to speak calmly and honestly
Keep beside your writing desk to unblock words
Carry during exams or interviews to steady nerves
Place on the throat during meditation
Add to a spell jar for clear communication between quarrelling friends
substituteNotes: Lapis Lazuli and Azurite share its royal blue wisdom, while Blue Lace Agate, Blue Kyanite and Amazonite also open the throat for calm communication.
cleansing: Brief rinse is fine; avoid soaking and salt. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight. Sun-safe.
whereToFind: Brazil, Canada (Ontario, Bancroft), Namibia, Greenland, Bolivia and India. Affordable and widely sold.
caution: Avoid soaking; it is softer than quartz and can scratch. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Late summer into autumn, season of Virgo (late Aug–Sep); Wednesdays
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Turquoise
mineral: Hydrated copper aluminium phosphate
colors: sky blue to robin's-egg blue and apple green, often with brown or black matrix
description: One of the first gemstones ever mined, turquoise was worked in Sinai by the Egyptians before 3000 BCE and set into the funeral mask of Tutankhamun. To the Navajo and Pueblo peoples it is a living stone of the sky and water, and to Persians it guarded against the evil eye. Its name means 'Turkish stone', for the trade route that carried it to Europe; horsemen tied it to their bridles for safe riding.
metaphysicalUses: Turquoise is a master healer and an ancient protective amulet. It guards travellers, especially riders and pilots, and is said to change colour to warn of danger or illness. It brings luck, strengthens friendship and honest communication, and links earth and sky. Because it is sacred to Native American and Persian peoples, many practitioners honour that heritage by buying from Indigenous artists.
uses: Wear while travelling for safe journeys
Give as a gift of friendship, as tradition says turquoise gifted brings more luck than turquoise bought
Place on the throat for honest, healing words
Carry as a talisman against the evil eye
Set on a healing altar with herbs for recovery
substituteNotes: Amazonite, Chrysocolla and Larimar share its blue-green sky-and-sea energy, Aquamarine protects travellers, and Malachite is its copper-bearing cousin.
cleansing: Porous: NOT water-safe for soaking, and keep it away from oils, lotions, salt and chemicals, which discolour it. Avoid prolonged sunlight, which can fade or crack it. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight.
whereToFind: Iran (Nishapur), the American Southwest (Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico), China, Egypt (Sinai) and Mexico. Much 'turquoise' is dyed howlite or magnesite or stabilised with resin; buy from licensed Native artists or reputable dealers.
caution: Contains copper. Porous; avoid water, oils and sun. Often stabilized with resin, dyed, or faked with dyed howlite. Toxic if swallowed or if its dust is inhaled: never use it in direct elixirs, drinking water or bath water (indirect method only, sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children (choking hazard); never cut, sand or grind it; its dust is harmful to inhale.
bestTime: Late autumn, season of Sagittarius (late Nov–Dec), its traditional birthstone month
pets: Keep away from pets; chewing or licking it can release toxic metal, and a swallowed stone can block the intestines.

name: Malachite
mineral: Copper carbonate hydroxide
colors: vivid emerald to forest green in swirling concentric bands
description: Ancient Egyptians ground malachite as eye paint and wore it to ward off evil, and in medieval Europe it was hung on children's cradles to frighten off bad spirits. Russia's Ural mines yielded such huge masses that the Tsars lined the Malachite Room of the Winter Palace with it. Its bands record the growth of copper-rich layers like the rings of a tree.
metaphysicalUses: Malachite is a fierce stone of change. It draws out old pain, breaks unwanted ties and patterns, and pushes toward transformation, sometimes uncomfortably fast. It was carried as protection against the evil eye, said to shatter as a warning of danger, and is used to protect during travel and to bless businesses. Midwives carried it to ease labour. Work with it when you are ready for real change.
uses: Keep a polished piece on the desk to draw business success (handle polished only)
Hold over the heart during release rituals to draw out old hurt
Place in a sealed charm bag for travel protection
Set on the altar during transformation rites at the new moon
Display a polished slice in the home as a guardian against the evil eye
substituteNotes: Green Aventurine, Emerald and Jade share its green Venusian heart energy, Chrysocolla is its copper cousin, and Moss Agate brings growth.
cleansing: NOT water-safe: it is soft and porous, and water, salt and acids damage it and can release copper. Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight or on selenite. Avoid long sunlight, which can dull it.
whereToFind: Democratic Republic of Congo (most today), Zambia, Russia (Urals), Australia and Arizona (USA). Congolese copper mining has serious labour and child-safety concerns; seek traceable sources.
caution: Contains copper; wash hands after handling raw pieces and handle only polished stones for ritual. Not water-safe. Toxic if swallowed or if its dust is inhaled: never use it in direct elixirs, drinking water or bath water (indirect method only, sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Never cut, sand or grind it; its dust is harmful to inhale.
bestTime: Spring, Ostara to Beltane (Mar–May), the green season of renewal
pets: Keep away from pets; chewing or licking it can release toxic metal, and a swallowed stone can block the intestines.

name: Azurite
mineral: Copper carbonate hydroxide, Cu3(CO3)2(OH)2 (a different mineral from malachite)
colors: intense midnight to azure blue, often with green malachite
description: Azurite takes its name from the Persian lazhward, blue. Egyptians and Mayans prized it as a sacred stone of the heavens and inner sight, and Chinese texts called it the Stone of Heaven. Ground azurite was a leading blue pigment of medieval painters. Over time azurite naturally converts to malachite, so the two are often found entwined.
metaphysicalUses: Azurite is a stone of insight and psychic awakening. It stimulates the third eye and intuition, clears confused thought, and brings flashes of understanding. Used by priests and seers as a stone of guidance, it deepens meditation and divination and helps one face hidden truths. Combined with malachite it unites vision with transformation.
uses: Place on the third eye during meditation or trance (dry, polished stone only)
Keep beside your divination tools to sharpen insight
Hold while studying complex occult texts
Set under the pillow (in a pouch) for revealing dreams
Use in a grid for spiritual guidance before a big decision
substituteNotes: Lapis Lazuli and Sodalite are deep blue stones of mind and insight, Blue Kyanite and Amethyst open intuition, and Malachite is its mineral twin.
cleansing: NOT water-safe and not sun-safe: water, salt and heat can damage it, and sunlight and heat can darken it. Cleanse with smoke, sound or on selenite.
whereToFind: Morocco, China, Mexico, Namibia, Arizona and Utah (USA), and Chessy in France. Buy from mineral dealers who know its provenance.
caution: Contains copper; wash hands after handling raw specimens. Not water- or sun-safe; very soft and fragile. Toxic if swallowed or if its dust is inhaled: never use it in direct elixirs, drinking water or bath water (indirect method only, sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Never cut, sand or grind it; its dust is harmful to inhale.
bestTime: Winter, season of Aquarius (late Jan–Feb)
pets: Keep away from pets; chewing or licking it can release toxic metal, and a swallowed stone can block the intestines.

name: Green Aventurine
mineral: Quartzite (quartz) with fuchsite mica inclusions
colors: soft mint to deep green with a glittering mica shimmer (aventurescence)
description: Aventurine shares its name with Italian 'aventurine glass', created a ventura, by chance, when Venetian glassmakers spilled copper filings into molten glass. The natural stone's sparkle comes from tiny green fuchsite flakes. Tibetans set it in the eyes of statues to see clearly, and gamblers have long rubbed it for luck.
metaphysicalUses: Green aventurine is the luckiest of all stones. It draws good fortune, opportunity and money, making it a favourite for job-seeking, competitions and games of chance. It also soothes the heart and encourages growth, optimism and new beginnings. Use it in money bowls, luck charms, green candle spells and gardening magic.
uses: Carry in your pocket for luck at interviews, auditions or the lottery
Place in the soil of a money plant to grow prosperity
Add to a money bowl with coins, cinnamon and basil
Hold while writing a job application
Tuck in a green mojo bag with a lucky dime and a bay leaf
substituteNotes: Jade is the other great green luck stone, Citrine and Pyrite draw money, and Peridot and Moss Agate bring green abundance and growth.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe (though very long sun may lighten it). Cleanse in running water, sunlight, moonlight or smoke.
whereToFind: India (most commercial supply), Brazil, Russia and Chile. Very affordable; dyed quartz and green aventurine glass are sold as fakes.
caution: Its green color comes from chromium-bearing fuchsite mica; some 'aventurine' is dyed quartz or glass. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Spring, Ostara to Beltane (Mar–May); Thursdays and Wednesdays
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Jade
mineral: Two minerals: nephrite (amphibole, calcium magnesium iron silicate) and jadeite (pyroxene, sodium aluminium silicate)
colors: creamy white to lavender and every green from apple to imperial emerald
description: In China jade has been revered for over 7,000 years as the essence of heaven and earth, a stone of virtue, longevity and immortality, carved into burial suits for princes. The Maori carve nephrite pounamu into treasured hei-tiki and toki heirlooms, and Spanish conquistadors called it piedra de ijada, loin stone, for its supposed kidney cures. Its toughness makes it nearly impossible to break.
metaphysicalUses: Jade is a stone of serene good fortune. It draws prosperity, protects its wearer, and brings long life, wisdom and balance. Placed under the pillow it is said to bring insightful dreams; carried, it keeps one calm and lucky. It is especially honoured in Chinese and Maori traditions, where a piece of jade given as a gift carries the love and protection of the giver. Use it in money, longevity and harmony magic.
uses: Wear a jade bangle or pendant as a lifelong protection and luck charm
Place under the pillow for dreams of insight
Hold during prosperity meditation and visualise growth
Keep in the home to harmonise family relationships
Gift a carved piece to bless a child or elder with long life (keep small pieces away from children under 3)
Set in a garden as a blessing on growing things
substituteNotes: Green Aventurine is the other classic luck stone, Emerald and Malachite share its green Venus energy, and Moss Agate and Prehnite bring its gentle earthy harmony.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe (nephrite and jadeite are very tough). Cleanse in running water, moonlight or smoke. Avoid harsh chemicals on treated jade.
whereToFind: Jadeite: Myanmar (Burma), Guatemala, Japan. Nephrite: British Columbia (Canada), New Zealand, Siberia, China, Wyoming. Myanmar jade can fund conflict; much 'jade' is dyed or bleached, or is serpentine or glass, so buy certified 'Type A' from reputable sources.
caution: Often imitated, dyed or polymer-impregnated; insist on honest labeling. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Spring, around Beltane (Apr–May) and Lunar New Year
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Tiger's Eye
mineral: Quartz (silicon dioxide) intergrown with crocidolite (blue asbestos) fibres, coloured by iron oxides
colors: golden brown to honey with shimmering bands (chatoyancy); blue (hawk's eye) and red varieties
description: Roman soldiers carried tiger's eye engraved with protective symbols, believing it let them see in all directions during battle. In Egypt it was set into the eyes of deity statues to express divine vision. Its silky moving bands of light come from fibrous mineral structures, giving it the look of a watchful cat's eye.
metaphysicalUses: Tiger's eye brings the clarity of the sun down into the solid earth. It lends courage, self-confidence and willpower, guards against the evil eye and curses, and helps one see a situation clearly without being ruled by fear. It is also a stone of practical wealth and good luck in business. Use it when you must act boldly, make decisions, or stand firm.
uses: Carry as an amulet against the evil eye and ill-wishing
Wear on the solar plexus in interviews or negotiations for confidence
Place in the wallet or cash register to attract money
Hold while making decisions to see clearly
Use in a courage spell with an orange candle on a Sunday
substituteNotes: Citrine, Carnelian and Sunstone share its solar fire and courage, Pyrite brings luck and wealth, and Smoky Quartz grounds as it does.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe. Cleanse in running water, sunlight, smoke or sound.
whereToFind: South Africa (Northern Cape), Western Australia, India, Namibia, Brazil and Myanmar. Heated tiger's eye becomes red 'bull's eye'.
caution: Polished stones are safe to handle, but rough tiger's eye contains crocidolite (blue asbestos) fibers: never cut, sand or grind raw tiger's eye, as the dust can cause serious lung disease. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them.
bestTime: High summer, the season of Leo (late Jul–Aug), Lughnasadh
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Carnelian
mineral: Chalcedony (microcrystalline quartz) coloured by iron oxide
colors: translucent orange to blood red and amber
description: Egyptians placed carnelian amulets called tyet, the Knot of Isis, on mummies to protect the dead on their journey, and they believed it calmed anger and jealousy. Napoleon carried a carnelian seal throughout his campaigns, and the Prophet Muhammad was said to wear a carnelian ring. Medieval alchemists used it to boost the power of other stones.
metaphysicalUses: Carnelian is a stone of fire in the belly. It restores vitality and motivation, stirs creativity and sensuality, and bolsters courage for performing, speaking and taking risks. It is used to protect the home from intruders, misfortune and envy, and for fertility and passion magic. Wear it when you need to act, create or shine.
uses: Wear while performing, singing or public speaking
Place on the sacral chakra to unblock creativity
Keep by the front door as an old protection against envy and theft
Add to a lust or passion charm with cinnamon and red rose
Carry on long tiring days for stamina
Set on a fertility altar with an egg and seeds
substituteNotes: Red Jasper, Orange Calcite, Sunstone, Fire Agate and Garnet all carry warm sacral fire, courage and vitality.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe. Cleanse in running water, sunlight or smoke; charge in morning sun.
whereToFind: India, Brazil, Uruguay, Madagascar and Indonesia. Much carnelian is heat-treated agate dyed orange; natural stones show cloudy, uneven colour.
caution: Much carnelian sold is dyed or heat-treated agate. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Summer, Litha to Lughnasadh (Jun–Aug); Tuesdays and Sundays
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Red Jasper
mineral: Microcrystalline quartz (chalcedony) with iron oxide (hematite) inclusions; an opaque rock
colors: brick red to rust and earthy brown red, sometimes with brecciated veins
description: Jasper was one of the twelve stones on the breastplate of the Hebrew High Priest and one of the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem in Revelation. Native American traditions used it as a rain-bringing and dowsing stone, and Egyptians carved red jasper into the tyet amulet of Isis. It has been used as a protective stone for warriors and as a seal for millennia.
metaphysicalUses: Red jasper is the steady, nurturing warrior stone. It grounds the body and grants stamina, endurance and quiet courage, rather than flashy fire. It protects against harm, steadies the emotions under stress, and rekindles passion. It is a stone for long efforts, physical recovery, and rooting a spell firmly in the material world.
uses: Carry during long workdays or physical labour for stamina
Place at the root chakra in meditation to feel rooted
Bury at the boundaries of a garden or home for protection
Hold during dream work to recall dreams
Add to a passion or vitality charm with ginger and cinnamon
substituteNotes: Carnelian and Garnet share its red vitality, Bloodstone its Martial strength, and Hematite and Smoky Quartz its grounding.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe. Cleanse in running water, earth, smoke or sunlight.
whereToFind: India, Brazil, South Africa, Madagascar, Russia and the USA. Very affordable and widely available.
caution: Some red jasper is dyed. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Spring, season of Aries (late Mar–Apr); Tuesdays
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Bloodstone
mineral: Chalcedony (microcrystalline quartz) coloured green by chlorite or hornblende with red iron oxide spots
colors: deep forest green speckled with blood-red jasper spots
description: Medieval Christian legend held that bloodstone formed when drops of Christ's blood fell on green jasper at the foot of the cross. Its old name heliotrope, 'sun turner', comes from the belief that in water it turned the sun's reflection red. Babylonians carved it into seals, and soldiers carried it to stanch wounds and give courage.
metaphysicalUses: Bloodstone is a stone of brave hearts and strong blood. It lends courage and endurance in the face of adversity, helps athletes and warriors to victory, and is used in healing magic for the blood and vitality. Old grimoires say it brings legal success, money, and even invisibility and weather-working. It purifies and grounds while keeping the heart open.
uses: Carry during competitions or confrontations for victory
Add to healing spells for recovery and vitality
Place on legal papers or carry to court for justice
Keep in a money pouch for prosperity
Wear during difficult times for steadfast courage
substituteNotes: Red Jasper and Garnet carry its red vitality, Green Aventurine and Jade its green prosperity, and Hematite its old bloodstone name and strength.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe. Cleanse in running water, earth or smoke.
whereToFind: India (most common source), Brazil, Australia, China and the USA. Affordable; look for clear red spots on dark green.
caution: Generally durable; avoid hard knocks. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Early spring, the season of Aries (Mar–Apr), and around Easter and Ostara
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Garnet
mineral: Garnet group silicates (almandine, pyrope, spessartine, grossular and others)
colors: wine red to deep crimson; also orange, green (tsavorite) and colour-change
description: Garnet's name comes from the Latin granatum, pomegranate, for its resemblance to the fruit's seeds, and it is linked to Persephone, who ate pomegranate seeds in the underworld. Legend says Noah hung a glowing garnet in the Ark to light the way, and medieval travellers carried it to illuminate the night and protect against harm. Anglo-Saxon goldsmiths set thousands of garnets into the Sutton Hoo treasures.
metaphysicalUses: Garnet is the stone of passionate, committed love and of vital life-force. It deepens devotion and fidelity, rekindles desire, and is exchanged by those parting to ensure reunion. It is an old travel talisman, especially against harm at night, and it grants strength and success in business. Through Persephone it also connects to underworld journeys and the cycles of descent and return.
uses: Exchange garnets with a loved one before a separation to ensure a return
Wear for passion or add to a lust spell with red candles
Carry while travelling, especially at night
Place on the altar for Persephone during autumn rites
Hold at the root chakra to restore vitality after illness
substituteNotes: Ruby, Red Jasper and Carnelian share its red fire and passion, Bloodstone its vitality, and Rhodonite its loving heart energy.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe. Cleanse in running water, sunlight, smoke or sound.
whereToFind: India, Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Tanzania, Brazil, the Czech Republic (Bohemian pyrope) and the USA. Generally affordable and ethically available.
caution: Generally durable; avoid hard knocks and sudden heat. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Winter, the season of Capricorn into January (its birthstone month); also Samhain for Persephone work
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Ruby
mineral: Corundum (aluminium oxide) coloured by chromium
colors: pinkish red to deep 'pigeon's blood' crimson
description: In Sanskrit ruby is ratnaraj, king of gems. Burmese warriors inserted rubies under their skin to become invulnerable, and medieval Europeans believed it darkened to warn of danger and kept the wearer safe from plague and poison. It glows red under ultraviolet light because of its chromium content, as if it holds a fire within.
metaphysicalUses: Ruby is the royal stone of passion and life-force. It fills the heart with fiery love and desire, grants courage and leadership, and draws wealth and success. It protects its wearer, especially their home and possessions, and restores energy and motivation. Work ruby in spells for passionate love, personal power and sovereignty.
uses: Wear over the heart to kindle passion in a relationship
Place on a sun or sovereignty altar during Litha
Carry for courage when stepping into leadership
Set beside a red candle in a vitality or healing spell
Keep in a jewellery box to protect wealth and possessions
substituteNotes: Garnet is the classic affordable red substitute, Carnelian and Red Jasper share its fire, and Rhodonite and Sunstone carry its heart and solar energy.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe (very hard). Cleanse in running water, sunlight or smoke. Fracture-filled or glass-filled rubies should be kept from heat and chemicals.
whereToFind: Myanmar (Mogok), Mozambique, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Madagascar and Greenland. Burmese rubies have been subject to sanctions over human rights; ask for origin and treatment disclosure.
caution: Many rubies are lead-glass filled; avoid heat and acids on such stones and never put them in elixirs. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Midsummer, Litha (Jun) and July, its birthstone month
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Emerald
mineral: Beryl (beryllium aluminium silicate) coloured by chromium and vanadium
colors: vivid grass green to deep bluish green, often with inclusions called 'jardin'
description: Cleopatra claimed Egypt's emerald mines as her own and gave carved emeralds to visiting dignitaries. The Romans dedicated it to Venus, and ancient lore held that a serpent gazing upon an emerald would be blinded. The Inca and Muisca of Colombia used emeralds in sacred ceremony for centuries before the Spanish arrived. The tiny inclusions inside most emeralds are lovingly called their garden.
metaphysicalUses: Emerald is the stone of successful, faithful love and of Venusian abundance. It deepens loyalty and domestic bliss, draws prosperity and growth, and was believed to reveal truth and grant foresight when placed under the tongue. It soothes the heart, brings wisdom and patience, and supports recovery. Use it in marriage, love and prosperity magic, and on Venus's day.
uses: Wear on a Friday to draw faithful love
Place in a handfasting or marriage blessing ritual
Add a small rough emerald to a money or abundance grid
Meditate with it at the heart for patience and healing
Keep with the household papers to bless family finances
substituteNotes: Green Aventurine, Jade, Malachite and Peridot carry emerald's green Venusian energy, and Rose Quartz shares its love work.
cleansing: Most emeralds are oil- or resin-treated: avoid hot water, soaking, ultrasonic cleaners and solvents. Wipe with a damp cloth. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight. Avoid prolonged heat and sun.
whereToFind: Colombia (Muzo, Chivor), Zambia, Brazil, Afghanistan, Ethiopia and Zimbabwe. Rough emerald in matrix is affordable; seek traceable mines and treatment disclosure.
caution: Brittle with many inclusions and usually oil- or resin-treated; avoid knocks, heat and solvents. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Spring, Beltane (May 1) and May, its birthstone month; Fridays
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Sapphire
mineral: Corundum (aluminium oxide) coloured by iron and titanium
colors: cornflower to midnight blue; also pink, yellow, padparadscha and colourless
description: Ancient Persians believed the earth rested on a giant sapphire whose reflection coloured the sky. Greeks wore it when consulting the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, and medieval clergy wore blue sapphires as symbols of heaven. Kings wore it to protect against envy and harm, and it has crowned royal engagement rings for centuries.
metaphysicalUses: Sapphire is a stone of serene, disciplined wisdom. It opens the mind to higher truths, sharpens psychic perception and divination, and lends calm focus. It protects against envy, curses and deception, attracts patronage and favour, and supports justice. Its Saturnian depth makes it ideal for serious study, oaths and commitments.
uses: Wear when consulting oracles or reading cards for clear sight
Hold during meditation for insight and calm
Carry to court or legal meetings for justice and truth
Use to seal an oath or vow in ritual
Keep near study materials for deep focus
substituteNotes: Lapis Lazuli is the ancient 'sapphirus', Sodalite and Azurite share its blue wisdom, and Blue Kyanite and Aquamarine carry its throat and clarity energy.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe (very hard). Cleanse in running water, sunlight, moonlight or smoke.
whereToFind: Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Myanmar, Thailand, Australia, Kashmir and Montana (USA). Most are heat-treated; ask about origin and treatment, and consider Montana or Sri Lankan stones with traceable supply.
caution: Many sapphires are heat- or diffusion-treated; this is not a hazard but should be disclosed. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Early autumn, September (its birthstone month), around Mabon
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Aquamarine
mineral: Beryl (beryllium aluminium silicate) coloured by iron
colors: pale sea-glass blue to deep ocean teal
description: Its name means 'water of the sea' in Latin. Sailors believed it was the treasure of mermaids and carried it to calm storms and ensure safe return, and Roman fishermen called it a gift of Neptune. In the Middle Ages it was used as a scrying crystal and believed to rekindle the love of married couples.
metaphysicalUses: Aquamarine carries the calm of the sea. It soothes fear and anger, gives courage to speak one's truth gently, and protects travellers, especially on water. It cleanses the emotions, supports tears and release, and opens the heart and throat for compassionate communication. Use it in sea magic, travel charms and spells to cool tempers.
uses: Carry on boats, ferries or flights for safe travel
Place in a bowl of sea water on the altar for sea-witchcraft
Wear at the throat to speak truth calmly
Hold during anxious moments and breathe like waves
Use as a scrying stone by moonlight
Add to a spell to soothe a hot-tempered household
substituteNotes: Larimar and Blue Lace Agate share its sea-blue calm, Amazonite and Celestite soothe the throat and mind, and Moonstone carries its watery, travel-blessing energy.
cleansing: Water-safe; especially loves sea water or running water (rinse salt off after). Can fade in strong prolonged sunlight; charge under the moon.
whereToFind: Brazil, Madagascar, Mozambique, Nigeria, Pakistan, Namibia and Colorado (Mount Antero, USA). Usually heat-treated to remove green tones.
caution: Can fade in strong prolonged sunlight.
