Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Late winter into spring, March (its birthstone month), season of Pisces
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Fluorite
mineral: Calcium fluoride (CaF2)
colors: violet, green, blue, yellow, pink or clear, often banded like a rainbow
description: Fluorite gave its name to fluorescence, glowing under ultraviolet light, and its use as a flux (Latin fluere, to flow) in metal smelting gave it its own name. Romans carved banded Blue John from Derbyshire into luxurious drinking cups called murrhine vessels. Its perfect octahedral cleavage lets it be split by hand into natural eight-sided crystals.
metaphysicalUses: Fluorite brings order to chaos. It is the student's stone, helping absorb and organise information, focus during study and make decisions clearly. It shields against mental manipulation and psychic overwhelm, cleansing the aura of confusion and stagnant energy. Different colours lend different flavours: purple for intuition, green for heart healing, blue for communication.
uses: Keep on the desk while studying or working on complex tasks
Hold during decision-making to sort thoughts
Place beside a computer to tidy chaotic energy
Use a rainbow octahedron in meditation to balance all chakras
Carry in crowds to avoid psychic overwhelm
substituteNotes: Amethyst and Lepidolite carry its purple calm, Clear Quartz its clarity, Sodalite its rational focus, and Ametrine its balance of colours.
cleansing: Soft and brittle: brief rinse only, never soak, avoid salt. Not sun-safe, as colours fade in sunlight. Cleanse with smoke, sound or on selenite.
whereToFind: China, Mexico, Spain, England (Derbyshire, Cornwall, Weardale), Illinois (USA), Morocco and Argentina. Affordable; much is sold as tumbled stones and octahedrons.
caution: Fluorine-bearing; avoid inhaling dust. Soft and cleaves easily; colors fade in sunlight. Toxic if swallowed or if its dust is inhaled: never use it in direct elixirs, drinking water or bath water (indirect method only, sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Never cut, sand or grind it; its dust is harmful to inhale.
bestTime: Late summer into autumn, back-to-learning season (Aug–Sep); Wednesdays
pets: Keep away from pets; chewing or licking it can release toxic metal, and a swallowed stone can block the intestines.

name: Lepidolite
mineral: Lithium-rich mica (potassium lithium aluminium silicate)
colors: lilac, lavender and pinkish violet with a pearly, flaky sparkle
description: Lepidolite's name comes from the Greek lepidos, scale, for its glittering scale-like mica flakes. It is a natural source of lithium, the element used in modern medicine to stabilise mood, which has made it a beloved stone of calm. It often grows with pink tourmaline and quartz in granite pegmatites.
metaphysicalUses: Lepidolite is the soft lavender blanket of the crystal world. It eases anxiety, stress and overwhelm, smooths emotional ups and downs, and helps one move through change and transition gracefully. It brings restful sleep, gentle dreams and acceptance. Keep it by the bed, use it in peace spells, or hold it through times of upheaval.
uses: Keep beside the bed or under the pillow for restful sleep
Hold during anxious moments and slow your breathing
Carry through big transitions such as moving, divorce or new jobs
Place in a peace jar with lavender and chamomile
Meditate with it at the heart and crown together
substituteNotes: Amethyst and Charoite share its calming purple ray, Howlite soothes and aids sleep, and Rose Quartz and Kunzite comfort the heart.
cleansing: NOT water-safe: it is soft mica that flakes and degrades in water. Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight or selenite. Limit sun, which can fade it.
whereToFind: Brazil, Madagascar, Zimbabwe, Russia, Canada and the USA (California, Maine). Affordable; mined alongside lithium, so ask how it was sourced.
caution: Not water-safe; soft and flaky. Its lithium is not a medicine, and it also contains aluminum and fluorine. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Autumn, season of Libra (late Sep–Oct)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Howlite
mineral: Calcium borosilicate hydroxide
colors: chalky white to grey with dark grey or black web-like veining
description: Howlite was discovered in Nova Scotia in 1868 by the Canadian chemist Henry How, who found it in a gypsum quarry. Because it is porous, it absorbs dye beautifully and is the most common imitation of turquoise and lapis. Undyed, its quiet white-and-grey veins have made it a favourite gentle stone for rest.
metaphysicalUses: Howlite calms an overactive mind and a quick temper. It teaches patience, eases insomnia caused by racing thoughts, and helps us speak and act thoughtfully rather than react. It supports memory and study, aids meditation, and helps release old resentments. Keep it by the bed, in the pocket of anyone who needs to slow down, or under the pillow for dreamy peace.
uses: Place under the pillow or in a pillowcase pouch for sleep
Hold to calm anger before responding to a provocation
Keep on the desk to remember what you study
Use in a patience spell with a white candle
Carry when practising mindful speech
substituteNotes: Lepidolite and Amethyst calm and bring sleep, Selenite and Moonstone carry its soft white lunar peace, and Snowflake Obsidian its black-on-white balance.
cleansing: Porous: brief rinse only, do not soak or use salt; dyed howlite may bleed. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight. Sun-safe.
whereToFind: Canada (Nova Scotia), California (USA), Turkey and Mexico. Cheap and widely available; be aware dyed howlite is sold as turquoise.
caution: Often dyed to imitate turquoise or lapis; label carefully. Porous and soft. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Late summer, season of Virgo (Aug–Sep), and at any time of stress
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Amazonite
mineral: Microcline feldspar (potassium aluminium silicate) coloured by lead and water
colors: soft turquoise to sea green with white streaks
description: Named after the Amazon River, though none has ever been found there, amazonite has been carved for millennia. It was one of the stones of Egypt, appearing in jewellery of Tutankhamun and possibly on the Book of the Dead's sacred tablets. Legend tied it to the Amazon warrior women, and Brazilian lore links it to the river's spirits.
metaphysicalUses: Amazonite is a stone of courageous truth. It helps us find our voice and set boundaries, calms the nerves and soothes the emotions, and balances masculine and feminine energies. It is also called a lucky stone for gamblers and new ventures. Use it for honest communication, hope during hard times, and protection from energetic overload.
uses: Wear at the throat to speak up and set boundaries
Carry for luck in new ventures or games of chance
Place near Wi-Fi routers or screens to calm the atmosphere
Hold during meditation to soothe worry
Add to a hope spell during the waxing moon
substituteNotes: Turquoise and Chrysocolla share its blue-green throat energy, Aquamarine and Blue Lace Agate its calm communication, and Green Aventurine its luck.
cleansing: Brief rinse is fine; avoid soaking and salt (it cleaves and may contain lead). Avoid long sun, which can fade it. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight.
whereToFind: Brazil, Madagascar, Russia, Colorado (Pikes Peak, USA), Ethiopia and Mozambique. Affordable; dyed and glass fakes exist.
caution: Contains trace lead; wash hands after handling raw pieces. Has perfect cleavage and can break if knocked. Toxic if swallowed or if its dust is inhaled: never use it in direct elixirs, drinking water or bath water (indirect method only, sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Never cut, sand or grind it; its dust is harmful to inhale.
bestTime: Late summer, season of Virgo (Aug–Sep), and Aquarius (Jan–Feb)
pets: Keep away from pets; chewing or licking it can release toxic metal, and a swallowed stone can block the intestines.

name: Chrysocolla
mineral: Hydrated copper silicate
colors: turquoise blue to sea green, often mottled with brown or black
description: Chrysocolla's name comes from the Greek chrysos, gold, and kolla, glue, as it was once used to solder gold. Cleopatra was said to have carried it to stay calm and gracious under pressure, and it has long been linked to wise women and goddess teachings. It forms where copper deposits weather, often alongside malachite and azurite.
metaphysicalUses: Chrysocolla is the stone of the wise woman and the gentle teacher. It eases heartache, softens tension, and encourages compassionate, clear speech. It connects us with the Divine Feminine, earth wisdom and the rhythms of nature. It is ideal for teachers, counsellors and anyone who must speak from the heart with grace.
uses: Carry when teaching or counselling for compassionate speech
Place on a goddess altar with sea shells
Hold over the heart to soothe heartbreak
Keep in a pocket to remain calm and gracious under stress
Use in a peace spell for a household in conflict
substituteNotes: Turquoise, Amazonite and Larimar share its blue-green calm, and Malachite and Azurite are its copper siblings.
cleansing: NOT water-safe: soft and porous, and contains copper. Avoid salt and chemicals. Avoid prolonged sun, which can dry and crack it. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight.
whereToFind: Peru, Chile, Congo, Mexico, Israel (Eilat stone) and Arizona (USA). Ask about copper-mine origins; much is stabilised or dyed.
caution: Contains copper; wash hands after handling raw pieces. Not water-safe. Toxic if swallowed or if its dust is inhaled: never use it in direct elixirs, drinking water or bath water (indirect method only, sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Never cut, sand or grind it; its dust is harmful to inhale.
bestTime: Spring into early summer, Beltane to Litha (May–Jun)
pets: Keep away from pets; chewing or licking it can release toxic metal, and a swallowed stone can block the intestines.

name: Rhodonite
mineral: Manganese silicate (pyroxenoid)
colors: rose pink to raspberry red with black manganese oxide veins
description: Rhodonite's name comes from the Greek rhodon, rose. In Russia it was adored by the Tsars, and the sarcophagus of Tsarina Maria Alexandrovna was carved from a single block of it. Russian lore called it orletz, eagle, because eagles were said to bring it to their nests. It is the official gemstone of Massachusetts.
metaphysicalUses: Rhodonite is first aid for the heart. It heals emotional wounds and old abuse, encourages forgiveness of self and others, and helps reconciliation after conflict. Its black veins ground love in the practical, so it supports healthy relationships rather than fantasy. It also gives courage to face pain, and is used to calm panic in emergencies.
uses: Hold during forgiveness or reconciliation rituals
Carry through the aftermath of a breakup
Place in a honey jar to sweeten a soured friendship
Rest on the heart during shadow work around old hurts
Keep in a first aid kit as an emotional rescue stone
substituteNotes: Rhodochrosite, Rose Quartz, Kunzite and Morganite share its pink heart healing, and Garnet carries its grounded red love.
cleansing: Water-safe briefly; avoid soaking and salt. Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight. Avoid long sun, which can fade the pink.
whereToFind: Russia (Urals), Australia, Peru, Brazil, Madagascar, Sweden and Massachusetts (USA). Affordable and widely sold.
caution: Manganese-bearing; can fade in long sun. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Spring, around Beltane (May) and Valentine's season (Feb)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Rhodochrosite
mineral: Manganese carbonate
colors: candy pink to raspberry red, often banded with white like agate
description: The Incas believed rhodochrosite was the solidified blood of their ancient rulers, and its banded stalactites from Argentinian mines are called Rosa del Inca. The Sweet Home mine in Colorado has produced world-famous ruby-red crystals. Its name comes from the Greek for rose-coloured.
metaphysicalUses: Rhodochrosite heals the inner child and teaches the heart to love without fear. It brings old emotional pain to the surface gently, so it can be released, and replaces it with joy, compassion and self-worth. It attracts a soul mate and kindles passion while keeping love joyful. Use it for self-love, recovering from heartbreak, and inner child work.
uses: Hold over the heart in inner child meditation
Carry when dating again after heartbreak
Place in a self-love bath sachet (outside the water, not submerged)
Add to a love-drawing altar with pink candles and rose petals
Wear to keep spirits bright through grief
substituteNotes: Rose Quartz, Rhodonite, Kunzite and Morganite share its pink heart medicine, and Garnet its passionate warmth.
cleansing: NOT water-safe for soaking: it is soft and reacts with acids and salt. Brief damp wipe only. Avoid sunlight and heat, which can fade it. Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight or selenite.
whereToFind: Argentina (Catamarca), Peru, South Africa, Colorado (Sweet Home mine, USA), Mexico and China. Mostly ethically mined by small operations; prices rise for gem crystals.
caution: Soft and acid-sensitive; avoid water, salt and lemon cleaners. Manganese-bearing. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Summer, season of Leo (late Jul–Aug)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Kunzite
mineral: Spodumene (lithium aluminium silicate), pink variety coloured by manganese
colors: pale pink to lilac and violet, glassy and often striated
description: Kunzite was named for George Frederick Kunz, Tiffany & Co.'s legendary gemmologist, who described it in 1903 after its discovery in California. It is called the Evening Stone because it fades in sunlight and is best worn by candlelight. J.P. Morgan was an avid collector, and kunzite remains a jewel of unconditional love.
metaphysicalUses: Kunzite is the stone of unconditional, divine love. It opens the heart to receive and give love, dissolves emotional blocks and old grief, and wraps the wearer in protective, peaceful energy. It calms anxiety, eases depression and helps one connect with the sacred. Use it in love spells of the higher heart and in rituals of comfort.
uses: Wear by evening during love rituals
Hold during heart meditation to feel unconditional love
Place beside a grieving person's bed
Carry through times of panic or depression
Set on the altar during devotional work to a love goddess
substituteNotes: Rose Quartz, Morganite and Rhodochrosite share its pink heart love, and Lepidolite and Amethyst its lilac calm and spiritual peace.
cleansing: Water-safe for brief rinses but cleaves easily, so handle gently. NOT sun-safe: it fades significantly in sunlight. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight.
whereToFind: Afghanistan, Brazil, Madagascar, Pakistan and California (Pala district, USA). Ask about origin; Afghan supply can be unregulated.
caution: Fades in sunlight; store in the dark. Perfect cleavage makes it fragile. Lithium-bearing. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children (choking hazard); do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.

name: Morganite
mineral: Beryl (beryllium aluminium silicate) coloured by manganese
colors: soft peach to salmon pink and rose
description: Morganite was named by George Kunz in 1911 after the financier J.P. Morgan, a patron of mineral collecting. It is the pink sister of emerald and aquamarine. Its gentle peachy glow has made it a modern favourite for engagement rings and heart magic.
metaphysicalUses: Morganite is a sweet, high-hearted love stone. It attracts love and maintains it, draws compassion and gentleness, and heals heartbreak with tender assurance. It invites angelic and divine love, calms stress, and helps us open our hearts after hurt. Use it in love-drawing spells, self-care rituals and blessing a new partnership.
uses: Wear when seeking a loving partner
Place in an engagement or handfasting blessing
Hold during self-love affirmations
Keep beside a bed to bring gentleness into a relationship
Add to an angel or devotional altar

name: Pyrite
mineral: Iron sulfide (FeS2)
colors: brassy metallic gold, sometimes iridescent; perfect cubes or 'suns'
description: Pyrite's name comes from the Greek pyr, fire, because it throws sparks when struck against iron, and it was used in early flintlock guns. The Inca and Aztecs polished it into mirrors for divination and healing. Gold-seekers called it fool's gold, but witches know it as one of the strongest money stones, and its perfect natural cubes still astonish collectors.
metaphysicalUses: Pyrite is a magnet for wealth and a shield for the self. It draws money, business success and abundance, boosts confidence and willpower, and deflects negative energy like a golden mirror. It brings Martial drive to manifest goals. Place it where money comes in, carry it into negotiations, and use it in protection spells of reflection.
uses: Keep a pyrite cube on the desk or by the till for money
Add to a money-drawing jar or green mojo bag
Carry into negotiations for confidence and favourable outcomes
Set on window ledges facing out to reflect harm
Use a polished pyrite mirror for scrying, as the Inca did
Place in a business blessing with a coin and basil
substituteNotes: Citrine and Tiger's Eye carry its golden money energy, Green Aventurine its luck, and Lodestone and Hematite its iron-born attraction and protection.
cleansing: NOT water-safe: it oxidises, rusts and can release sulfuric acid with moisture. Keep dry. Cleanse with smoke, sound or on selenite. Sun-safe.
whereToFind: Peru (Huanzala), Spain (Navajún cubes), Italy (Elba), China and the USA. Affordable; Spanish matrix cubes are a classic.
caution: Not water-safe; it oxidizes in moisture and humidity ('pyrite disease'), releasing sulfuric acid. It can contain traces of arsenic. Wash hands after handling. Toxic if swallowed or if its dust is inhaled: never use it in direct elixirs, drinking water or bath water (indirect method only, sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children (choking hazard); never cut, sand or grind it; its dust is harmful to inhale.
bestTime: High summer, Lughnasadh harvest (Aug); Sundays and Thursdays
pets: Keep away from pets; chewing or licking it can release toxic metal, and a swallowed stone can block the intestines.

name: Moss Agate
mineral: Chalcedony (microcrystalline quartz) with green chlorite or hornblende inclusions
colors: translucent white to clear with green moss-like or fern-like inclusions
description: Moss agate's tiny green inclusions look like moss, ferns or forests captured in ice. Farmers in Europe hung it on the horns of oxen or buried it in fields for a good harvest, and it was believed to be the stone of the land itself. Though named agate, it lacks agate's banding.
metaphysicalUses: Moss agate is the green witch's stone of growth. It blesses gardens, crops and houseplants, draws abundance and slow, steady prosperity, and connects to nature spirits and the fae. It brings emotional balance, helps new beginnings take root, and supports patience while things grow. Use it in garden magic, fertility work and earthy prosperity spells.
uses: Bury in garden beds or plant pots for healthy growth
Carry on forest walks to connect with nature spirits
Add to a fertility charm with seeds and an acorn
Place in a money bowl beside a growing plant
Hold while planting seeds of intention at the new moon
substituteNotes: Green Aventurine and Jade bring growth and abundance, Malachite its green change, and Unakite and Prehnite its earthy, nature-loving energy.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe. Cleanse in running water, earth (bury in the garden), sunlight or smoke.
whereToFind: India, Brazil, Uruguay, Australia and the USA (Montana, Wyoming). Affordable and plentiful.

Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.

name: Blue Lace Agate
mineral: Chalcedony (microcrystalline quartz), banded
colors: pale sky blue banded with white and lavender lace
description: Blue lace agate was discovered in Namibia in the 1960s, and its finest material came from a single mine there that has since closed. Its delicate bands resemble lace or waves on a sky-blue sea. Agates in general were used in ancient Mesopotamia as amulets, and blue agates were long believed to quench thirst and cool fevers.
metaphysicalUses: Blue lace agate is a gentle stone of calm, clear speech. It soothes anxiety, cools anger and helps us express feelings and truths kindly. It is a stone for teachers, public speakers and anyone who stammers or holds back their voice. Use it in communication spells, peace work and when you need gentle words after conflict.
uses: Wear at the throat when public speaking
Hold during a heartfelt conversation
Place on the throat chakra during meditation
Add to a peace jar for calm family communication
Carry to soothe nerves on stressful days
substituteNotes: Angelite, Celestite, Aquamarine and Larimar share its soft blue serenity, and Sodalite also opens the throat for communication.
cleansing: Water-safe. Cleanse in running water, smoke or moonlight. Avoid long sun, which can fade its delicate blue.
whereToFind: Namibia, South Africa, Malawi, Brazil and India. Much modern material is dyed; natural blue lace agate is pale and subtle.

name: Fire Agate
mineral: Chalcedony with layers of iron oxide (goethite or limonite) creating iridescence
colors: deep brown with flashes of fiery orange, red, gold and green
description: Fire agate formed 24 to 36 million years ago in the hot springs of the American Southwest and northern Mexico, where layers of iron oxide trapped light inside chalcedony bubbles. Skilled carvers grind away layers by hand to reveal its rainbow fire. Alchemists believed it held the essence of fire itself.
metaphysicalUses: Fire agate carries the flame of spirit. It protects by reflecting harm back to its source, burns away fear and lethargy, and kindles passion, sexuality and creative fire. It connects the root to the solar plexus, grounding power in the body. Use it in protection reversals, vitality spells and passion magic.
uses: Wear as a shield that reflects ill-will back to its source
Carry when you need courage and drive
Place near the bed to rekindle passion
Hold during candle magic to empower the flame
Use on a Mars or fire altar for strength workings
substituteNotes: Carnelian, Sunstone and Garnet share its fire and vitality, and Labradorite and Opal its flash of colour and protection.

name: Peridot
mineral: Olivine, gem variety (magnesium iron silicate)
colors: lime to olive green with a golden glow
description: Ancient Egyptians mined peridot on the island of Zabargad in the Red Sea, calling it the gem of the sun and gathering it at night when it glowed in the lamplight. Some of Cleopatra's famous 'emeralds' may have been peridot. It is one of the few gems that forms deep in the earth's mantle, and it also arrives on earth in meteorites.
metaphysicalUses: Peridot is a joyful stone of solar abundance. It attracts prosperity and success, protects against envy, nightmares and dark magic, and dispels jealousy and resentment. It opens the heart and lifts depression, helps release old burdens, and supports growth. Wear it set in gold for sun magic, or use it in prosperity and protection charms.

Place under the pillow to banish nightmares
Carry in a money pouch for growing prosperity
Hold during release rituals to let go of jealousy
Add to a Lughnasadh altar to celebrate abundance

bestTime: Late summer, August (its birthstone month), Lughnasadh

name: Prehnite
mineral: Calcium aluminium silicate hydroxide
colors: pale apple green to yellow-green, often with black epidote needles
description: Prehnite was the first mineral named after a person, Colonel Hendrik von Prehn, who brought it from the Cape of Good Hope in the 1780s. South African shamans are said to have used it in divination and to commune with ancestors. Its soft, grape-like botryoidal clusters look like bubbles of green light.
metaphysicalUses: Prehnite is the healer's companion, soothing and unconditional. It calms the anxious mind, brings peace with what is, and strengthens intuition and prophecy. It is said to protect healers and empaths from absorbing others' pain and to help connect with nature spirits and elementals. Use it in divination, lucid dreaming and healing rituals.
uses: Hold during healing sessions to protect your own energy
Place under the pillow for prophetic dreams
Meditate with it in a garden to meet nature spirits
Keep near divination tools to strengthen prophecy
Carry when facing a situation you must learn to accept

name: Celestite
mineral: Strontium sulfate
colors: pale sky blue to white, glassy, often in geodes
description: Named from the Latin caelestis, heavenly, for its sky-blue colour, celestite forms in geodes and limestone cavities. A geode in Put-in-Bay, Ohio, called Crystal Cave, is the world's largest. Strontium from celestite produces the brilliant red in fireworks.
metaphysicalUses: Celestite is a soft cloud of heavenly peace. It connects to angels, spirit guides and higher realms, calms anxious thoughts and supports dream recall and astral travel. It encourages gentle, honest communication and creates a tranquil atmosphere. Place a geode in a bedroom or meditation space and work with it in prayer and spirit-guide contact.
uses: Place a geode in the bedroom for peaceful sleep and dreams
Hold during prayer or guide meditations
Keep on the altar when calling on angels or spirits of air
Set beside a child's bed (out of reach) to soothe nightmares
Use in a blessing rite for a new home
substituteNotes: Angelite is its close sulfate cousin, Selenite and Danburite share its angelic light, and Blue Lace Agate and Aquamarine its soft blue serenity.

name: Angelite
mineral: Anhydrite (anhydrous calcium sulfate), blue variety
colors: pale periwinkle to lilac blue with white flecks
description: Angelite is compressed celestite and anhydrite formed over millions of years, found chiefly in Peru. The name was popularised in the 1980s, and it quickly became a stone of angelic communication. Its soft colour recalls a dawn sky.
metaphysicalUses: Angelite opens communication with angels, guides and the divine. It soothes anger and fear, brings tranquillity, and encourages compassionate speech. It helps those who struggle to express their feelings, and is used for telepathy and for creating a peaceful, protected space. Use it in prayer work, healing circles and gentle protection charms.

Place on the altar to invite guardian spirits
Keep near a meditation cushion for peaceful practice
Add to a blessing bag for a new baby (hung well out of the baby's reach) or a new home
Carry to stay calm when dealing with angry people

name: Blue Kyanite
mineral: Aluminium silicate (Al2SiO5)
colors: pale to deep sapphire blue, streaked and bladed with a pearly sheen
description: Kyanite's name comes from the Greek kyanos, deep blue. It has the odd property of being soft along its length and hard across it, which gave it the older name disthene, 'two strengths'. Fan-shaped black kyanite is called the witch's broom, and blue blades were used by ancient travellers as compasses when hung on a thread.
metaphysicalUses: Blue kyanite aligns the chakras and clears energy blockages instantly. It opens the throat for truthful expression and the third eye for psychic insight, supports dream recall and lucid dreaming, and calms. It is said never to hold negativity and so rarely needs cleansing. Use its blades to sweep energy, in communication spells and in meditation.

Place under the pillow for lucid and recalled dreams
Hold at the throat before public speaking
Lay along the spine during meditation
Carry when travelling as an old compass talisman

name: Orange Calcite
mineral: Calcium carbonate (CaCO3)
colors: translucent tangerine to honey orange, waxy
description: Calcite is one of the most common minerals on earth, the stuff of limestone, marble and cave formations. Its clear form (Iceland spar) shows double refraction and may have been the Viking 'sunstone' used to navigate on cloudy days. Orange calcite, largely from Mexico, is the cheerful sun of the family.
metaphysicalUses: Orange calcite is pure, bottled sunshine. It lifts depression and lethargy, kindles creativity, playfulness and sensuality, and boosts confidence. It cleanses stagnant energy and invites joy into the home. Use it in sun magic, creativity spells and any working where you need to feel bright and alive again.
uses: Place on a sunny windowsill in the kitchen to brighten the household
Hold at the sacral chakra to unblock creativity
Carry through the dark months to lift your mood
Add to a fertility or creativity altar with orange candles
Keep in a studio or craft space for playful inspiration
substituteNotes: Carnelian, Citrine, Sunstone, Amber and Fire Agate all carry its warm orange solar joy.

name: Sunstone
mineral: Feldspar (oligoclase or labradorite) with copper or hematite platelets causing aventurescence
colors: peach to orange and red with glittering golden spangles
description: Ancient Greeks believed sunstone brought the protection and vitality of Helios, and Indian lore says it shields against dark forces. Oregon sunstone, coloured by copper, is that state's official gem, and Native peoples there said it formed from the blood of a wounded warrior. Its golden sparkle seems to hold the summer sun.
metaphysicalUses: Sunstone brings the power of the sun to your spellwork. It lifts the spirits, banishes gloom and seasonal sadness, and empowers leadership, self-worth and independence. It draws good fortune and abundance, protects against those who drain energy, and fills you with warmth and optimism. Use it in Litha rites, success spells and confidence magic.

Carry in winter months to chase away seasonal gloom
Hold when stepping into leadership or self-employment
Place on a success altar with a gold candle
Charge in midsummer dawn light for maximum power
substituteNotes: Citrine, Carnelian, Orange Calcite, Tiger's Eye and Amber all carry warm solar fire and joy.

name: Unakite
mineral: Altered granite of pink orthoclase feldspar, green epidote and quartz
colors: mottled salmon pink and olive green
description: Unakite is named for the Unaka Mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee where it was first described. It forms when granite is altered by hydrothermal fluids, painting it in pink and green. Its mingled colours have made it a stone of balance between the heart and the earth.
metaphysicalUses: Unakite unites the heart and the third eye, balancing love with insight. It helps release blockages that stall growth, supports emotional healing and recovery, and is a traditional stone for fertility and healthy pregnancy. It grounds spiritual insight into daily life and helps reveal the root of patterns in shadow work.

Hold during shadow work to discover the root of a pattern
Place on the heart and third eye at once in meditation
Keep in a garden as a blessing on growth
Use in a healing spell for recovery after illness

name: Amber
mineral: Fossilised tree resin (organic mineraloid, succinite)
colors: honey yellow to cognac and cherry red; rarely blue or green; often with inclusions
description: Amber is resin from ancient forests, 25 to 50 million years old, sometimes holding trapped insects and leaves. The Greeks called it elektron, and rubbing it with wool produced the static that gave electricity its name. Norse lore said it was Freya's tears, wept for her wandering husband, and Baltic amber necklaces have been worn as protective amulets since the Stone Age. With jet it forms the traditional necklace of a high priestess.
metaphysicalUses: Amber holds the living light of ancient forests and the sun. It is a powerful protective amulet, drawing out negativity and illness, and a talisman of luck, beauty and vitality. It is a stone of the ancestors and of long memory. Wear it with jet to balance light and dark as a priestess, carry it for protection, and burn amber resin (not the gem) as incense for sun rites.
uses: Wear an amber and jet necklace during ritual as a priestess
Carry as a protective amulet and luck charm
Place on the altar at Litha to honour the sun
Use in beauty and glamour magic
Keep with ancestor relics to honour long memory
Rub with wool to raise a charge before casting
substituteNotes: Citrine, Sunstone, Orange Calcite and Carnelian carry its golden solar warmth, and Jet is its organic, protective partner.
cleansing: Soft and heat-sensitive: avoid soaking, salt, perfume, hot water and prolonged sun, which can cloud, crack or darken it. Wipe with a damp soft cloth. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight.
whereToFind: The Baltic coast (Poland, Lithuania, Russia's Kaliningrad), the Dominican Republic, Mexico (Chiapas) and Myanmar. Copal, plastic and pressed amber are common fakes; real amber floats in salt water and smells of pine resin when warmed.
caution: Amber teething necklaces are a choking and strangulation hazard and should never be used on babies or toddlers (FDA warning). Keep from heat, flame and solvents; amber is flammable. bestTime: Midsummer, Litha (Jun) and harvest-time Lughnasadh (Aug)

name: Opal
mineral: Hydrated amorphous silica (SiO2·nH2O), a mineraloid
colors: milky white, black, crystal or fiery orange with flashing rainbow play-of-colour
description: Romans prized opal as the symbol of hope and purity, and Pliny wrote that it held the fire of the carbuncle, the purple of amethyst and the green of emerald. Aboriginal Australian lore says the Creator came to earth on a rainbow, and where his foot touched the ground stones came alive with colour. A Walter Scott novel in 1829 gave it a false reputation for bad luck that crashed its European market. Its colour comes from light diffracting through tiny stacked silica spheres.
metaphysicalUses: Opal is a stone of enchantment and inner fire. It amplifies emotions and psychic gifts, and in old grimoires it was said to grant invisibility when wrapped in a bay leaf. It enhances glamour, beauty and allure, inspires creativity, and aids astral travel. Its watery nature mirrors the emotions back, so it supports transformation and emotional release. Work with it in glamour spells and spells of hope.

Wear during glamour or beauty rituals
Hold during astral travel or dream journeying
Keep in an artist's studio for inspiration
Place on the altar at Mabon for Libra-season love work
substituteNotes: Moonstone and Labradorite share its shimmering light, Fire Agate its play of fiery colour, Clear Quartz its versatility, and Rose Quartz its love.
cleansing: Opal contains water: avoid prolonged soaking (doublets and triplets must never be soaked), heat, sudden temperature changes and long sun, which can craze or crack it. A quick damp wipe is fine. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight.

name: Charoite
mineral: Complex potassium calcium sodium silicate
colors: lilac to deep purple with swirling silky chatoyant patterns, often with black and orange inclusions
description: Charoite is found in only one place on earth, the Chara River region of Siberia in Russia, and was officially described in 1978. Its swirling purple patterns look like smoke or dreams frozen in stone. Local lore says it was once called 'enchanted stone' by the people of Yakutia long before science named it.
metaphysicalUses: Charoite is the stone of soul-level transformation. It helps overcome fear, release resistance to change, and walk the spiritual path with courage. It protects against psychic attack, supports shadow work and helps process deep emotions, while encouraging sleep and calm dreams. Use it in transformation spells, initiation rites and spirit guide work.
uses: Hold during initiation or dedication rituals
Carry through life-changing transitions for courage
Place under the pillow (in a pouch) to quiet nightmares
Meditate with it during shadow work
Keep on the altar at Samhain as a stone of soul journeys
substituteNotes: Amethyst, Lepidolite and Fluorite share its purple spiritual energy, Labradorite its protective transformation, and Malachite its push toward change.
cleansing: Water-safe for brief rinses; avoid soaking and salt. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight. Avoid long sun which may fade it.
whereToFind: Only the Murun Massif near the Chara River, Sakha (Yakutia), Siberia, Russia. Supply is limited; dyed fakes and imitations exist.
caution: May fade in long sun; avoid soaking. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Samhain (Oct 31) and the season of Scorpio (Oct–Nov)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Larimar
mineral: Pectolite (sodium calcium silicate hydroxide), blue variety coloured by copper
colors: sea-foam turquoise to deep marine blue with white wave patterns
description: Larimar is found only in the mountains of the Dominican Republic. A local priest first noted it in 1916, and in 1974 Miguel Méndez named it by combining his daughter Larissa's name with mar, the Spanish word for sea. Islanders said the blue stones washed down from the sea and that it came from lost Atlantis.
metaphysicalUses: Larimar carries the healing calm of Caribbean waters. It soothes stress and anger, cools hot emotions, and supports gentle communication from the heart. It connects us to the sea, goddesses of water and the feminine divine, and helps release emotional baggage. Use it in sea-witchcraft, emotional healing and peace work.
uses: Hold at the throat to speak calmly in tense moments
Place on a sea altar with shells and salt water (stone kept dry)
Carry when anxious to recall the rhythm of waves
Wear during goddess or water devotions
Use in a release ritual at the waning moon
substituteNotes: Aquamarine, Turquoise, Blue Lace Agate, Chrysocolla and Amazonite share its sea-blue calm and throat-heart healing.
cleansing: Avoid soaking and salt; a quick rinse is fine. NOT sun-safe: it fades with prolonged sunlight. Cleanse with smoke, sound or moonlight.
whereToFind: Only the Barahona province of the Dominican Republic (Los Chupaderos mines). Buy from Dominican artisans to support local miners.
caution: Fades in prolonged sunlight; relatively soft. Its color comes from trace copper. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Summer, Litha to Lughnasadh (Jun–Aug), and the season of Pisces (Feb–Mar)
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Danburite
mineral: Calcium borosilicate
colors: water-clear to white, pale pink or champagne yellow
description: Danburite was first found in 1839 in Danbury, Connecticut, a site now buried under the town. Its striated prisms with wedge-shaped tips resemble topaz, and fine crystals now come from Mexico and Madagascar. In modern crystal lore it is a high-vibration stone of angels and light.
metaphysicalUses: Danburite fills the aura with clear, gentle light. It opens the crown and heart, connects with angels and higher guidance, and brings serenity, patience and acceptance. It is used to ease grief, support those near death, and clear karmic patterns. Place it at the crown in meditation or keep it near anyone who needs spiritual comfort.
uses: Hold at the crown during meditation for spiritual connection
Place beside a sick or dying person for peace
Use as a gentler alternative to clear quartz on the altar
Carry to ease grief and heartache
Add to a home blessing grid of white stones
substituteNotes: Clear Quartz, Selenite and Herkimer Diamond share its high-vibration clarity, Celestite its angelic light, and Rose Quartz its gentle heart energy.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe. Cleanse in running water, sunlight, moonlight or smoke.
whereToFind: Mexico (Charcas, San Luis Potosí), Madagascar, Japan, Russia, Myanmar and Tanzania. Moderately priced; look for clean, striated prisms.
caution: Brittle; avoid hard knocks. Never swallow it; a clean, untreated, unbroken stone is generally considered low risk for a direct elixir, but the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container) is safer. Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Midsummer, Litha (Jun) and the season of Leo
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Lodestone
mineral: Naturally magnetised magnetite (iron oxide, Fe3O4)
colors: dull black to dark grey-brown, often bristling with iron filings (magnetic sand)
description: Lodestone, 'leading stone', is magnetite magnetised, perhaps by lightning. Ancient Chinese diviners made the first compasses from lodestone spoons, and Greek sailors navigated by it. In hoodoo and folk magic, lodestones are kept as living spirits: they are paired, named, baptised and fed magnetic sand and whiskey or oil to keep drawing luck, love and money.
metaphysicalUses: Lodestone is a living magnet of the old ways. It is the great drawing stone: it pulls money, luck, love, customers and good fortune toward its keeper. Paired male and female lodestones are kept together in a red bag for fidelity and lasting love. In Southern conjure, lodestones are fed with magnetic sand and dressed with oils to stay strong. It also grounds and steers you toward your true path.
uses: Keep a pair in a red flannel bag for love and fidelity
Feed weekly with a pinch of magnetic sand to keep its pull strong
Carry in a gambler's mojo bag for luck
Dress with money-drawing oil and place under a green candle
Place by the shop door to draw customers
substituteNotes: Hematite and Pyrite are related iron minerals, Green Aventurine draws luck, Garnet love and fidelity, and Black Tourmaline its grounding.
cleansing: NOT water-safe: magnetite rusts. Keep dry. In folk tradition it is fed rather than cleansed; smoke or sound may also be used. Sun-safe.
whereToFind: Arkansas and New Jersey (USA), Sweden, Brazil and India; sold in botanicas and hoodoo supply shops. Many 'lodestones' are synthetic magnets; real ones collect fine iron sand.
caution: Keep magnets away from pacemakers, implanted devices, cards and electronics; not water-safe (rusts). Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Any season; traditionally fed on Fridays for love and Thursdays for money
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Hag Stone
mineral: Any stone (often flint, chalk or sandstone) with a naturally worn hole made by water or burrowing creatures
colors: beach grey, chalky white, flint black or tan, with a natural hole
description: A stone pierced naturally by water is one of the oldest charms in British and European folk magic. Lore says looking through the hole reveals faeries, spirits and witches, and that it protects against nightmares (the 'hag' who rides sleepers), the evil eye and enchantment. Welsh lore said adder stones formed from the breath of snakes, and they were hung over doors, beds and stable stalls to keep horses from being 'witch-ridden' at night.
metaphysicalUses: The hag stone is the witch's natural window into the Otherworld. Look through it to see faeries and spirits, or to reveal truth. Hung by the door, bed or on the keyring, it protects against nightmares, ill-wishing and malicious magic. It has been used to bless fertility, heal, and bring luck to boats and travellers. Hag stones must be found, not bought, by tradition; they are gifts from the water.
uses: Hang on a red cord over the bed to ward off nightmares
Look through it on a misty evening to glimpse the fae
Tie to the keyring for travel protection
Hang above the front door or in a barn as an old house charm
Hold up to the full moon and make a wish through the hole
Thread several on a cord to make a protective witch's ladder
substituteNotes: Staurolite is another natural folk amulet of faery lore, Black Tourmaline and Jet carry its protection, and Moonstone and Labradorite its Otherworldly sight.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe, being made by water; cleanse in sea water, running streams, moonlight or smoke. Chalk stones may soften if soaked.
whereToFind: Shingle beaches and riverbeds worldwide, especially the flint beaches of southern England, Cornwall, Brittany, Ireland and the Baltic. Tradition says to find your own; take only what you will use and respect protected beaches.
caution: Check local laws, as removing stones from some beaches is prohibited. Chalk and sandstone hag stones are soft and can crumble around the hole. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Beltane (May 1) and Samhain (Oct 31), when the faery realm is closest; also midsummer's eve
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Staurolite
mineral: Iron magnesium zinc aluminium silicate hydroxide; often forms twinned crosses
colors: reddish brown to dark brown, rough and opaque
description: Staurolite takes its name from the Greek stauros, cross, for its natural twin crystals that form a Greek cross or a St Andrew's X. Appalachian legend tells that faeries wept when they heard of the crucifixion, and their tears turned into these crosses, giving Fairy Stone State Park in Virginia its name. Presidents Roosevelt and Wilson are said to have carried them for luck.
metaphysicalUses: Staurolite is an old good-luck amulet and faery charm. It protects against accidents, illness and witchcraft, and travellers carried it for safe journeys. It connects to faery folk and earth spirits, grounds and calms, and is used to contact nature beings and the realms beyond. Wear it or carry it as a talisman of protection and blessing.
uses: Carry as a good-luck and safe-travel talisman
Wear on a cord as a protective amulet
Leave on a stump or under a hawthorn as an offering when calling the fae
Place on the altar as a natural equal-armed cross for the four elements
Bury at the corners of the home for earthy protection
substituteNotes: Hag Stone shares its faery folk-amulet lore, Moss Agate its nature spirits, Smoky Quartz and Black Tourmaline its grounding protection, and Jade its luck.
cleansing: Water-safe and sun-safe. Cleanse in running water, earth, sunlight or smoke.
whereToFind: Virginia (Fairy Stone State Park), Georgia and North Carolina (USA), Brazil, Russia and Switzerland. Carved 'fairy crosses' are sometimes faked from soft stone; real staurolite is hard and gritty.
caution: Often sold still in schist matrix, which crumbles. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Midsummer's eve (Jun) and Beltane (May), faery seasons
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.

name: Pearl
mineral: Organic gem of nacre (calcium carbonate as aragonite and conchiolin) formed in molluscs
colors: creamy white, pink, silver, gold and black with soft orient lustre
description: Pearls have been called the tears of the moon, the tears of the gods, and the tears of Aphrodite, who was born from the sea. Cleopatra famously dissolved a pearl in vinegar to win a bet with Mark Antony. Chinese legend says pearls fell from the sky when dragons fought, and they were believed to protect against fire and bring wisdom. Today most pearls are cultured.
metaphysicalUses: Pearl is the moon's own jewel and a stone of Aphrodite and sea goddesses. It brings beauty, grace, love and fertility, soothes the emotions, and deepens lunar and sea magic. It is said to bring luck and protect the wearer, especially near water. Wear pearls during full moon rituals, in glamour magic and in love spells.
uses: Wear during full moon esbats to honour the Moon
Place on an altar to Aphrodite or a sea goddess
Use in glamour and beauty spells for grace
Offer a pearl to the sea in gratitude for a granted wish
Keep in a fertility charm with a moonstone
substituteNotes: Moonstone and Selenite carry its lunar glow, Opal its iridescence, Rose Quartz its love and beauty, and Aquamarine its sea magic.
cleansing: Very soft and acid-sensitive: never soak, never use salt, vinegar, perfume or cleaners. Wipe with a soft damp cloth after wearing. Avoid heat and prolonged sun. Cleanse with moonlight or sound. Restring pearl strands periodically.
whereToFind: Cultured pearls from Japan (Akoya), China (freshwater), Tahiti (black), Australia and Indonesia (South Sea). Seek farms with sustainable practices; natural wild pearls are now extremely rare.
caution: Damaged by acids, perfume, sweat and dryness; put pearls on last and take them off first. Never swallow it, and do not put it directly in elixirs or drinking water; use only the indirect method (stone sealed in a separate glass container). Keep small stones away from young children, who can choke on them. Do not dry-cut, sand or grind it; stone dust harms the lungs, so use wet methods and a respirator.
bestTime: Midsummer, June (its birthstone month), season of Cancer
pets: Keep small stones away from pets that chew; a swallowed stone can block the intestines and may need surgery.
